slides.text: ﻿ INTRODUCTION  Network security is the set of strategies, policies, processes, and technologies designed to protect the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of a network architecture and its data. It encompasses both hardware and software solutions deployed to prevent, detect, and monitor unauthorized access, misuse, modification, or denial of a computer network and its accessible resources.

﻿ INTRODUCTION  Network security is structured around three primary layers of defense:
Physical Security: Preventing unauthorized physical access to network components like routers, switches, and cabling closets.
Technical Security: Deploying software and hardware mechanisms (such as firewalls, intrusion prevention systems, and encryption) to protect data stored on the network or in transit across it.
Administrative Security: Establishing organizational policies, user access controls, and training to govern how users interact with the network safely.

﻿ SECURITY GOALS Computer Security: 
The protection afforded to an automated information system in order to attain the applicable objectives of preserving the integrity, availability, and confidentiality of information system resources (includes hardware, software, firmware, information/data, and telecommunications). Ref: Special Publication 800-12: An Introduction to Computer Security - The NIST Handbook
﻿ CIA Triad

﻿ SECURITY GOALS Confidentiality: This term covers two related concepts:
Data confidentiality: Assures that private or confidential information is not made available or disclosed to unauthorized individuals.
Privacy is the rule/policy: It defines the legal, ethical, and structural boundaries of data ownership. It dictates what data an organization has the right to collect and who is authorized to see it.

Integrity: This term covers two related concepts:
Data integrity: Assures that information and programs are changed only in a specified and authorized manner.
System integrity: Assures that a system performs its intended function in an unimpaired manner, free from deliberate or unauthorized manipulation of the system.

Availability: Assures that systems work promptly, and service is not denied to authorized users. Ref: Cryptography and Network Security Principles and Practices, Fourth Edition By William Stallings

﻿ SECURITY ATTACKS Security Attacks can be classified into two types:
Passive Attack
Active Attack

﻿ PASSIVE ATTACK  The goal of the opponent is to obtain information that is being transmitted. 
Two types of passive attacks are the release of message contents (snooping) and traffic analysis.

﻿ ACTIVE ATTACK  Active attacks involve some modification of the data stream or the creation of a false data stream.
subdivided into four categories: masquerade, replay, modification of messages, and denial of service.
﻿ SECURITY ATTACKS

﻿ Snooping refers to unauthorized access to or interception of data. Traffic analysis  refers to obtaining some other type of information by monitoring online traffic.  Attacks Threatening Confidentiality

﻿ Modification means that the attacker intercepts the message and changes it. Masquerading or spoofing happens when the attacker impersonates somebody else. Replaying means the attacker obtains a copy of a message sent by a user and later tries to replay it.  Repudiation means that  sender of the message might later deny that she has sent the message; the receiver of the message might later deny that he has received the message. Attacks Threatening Integrity
﻿ Denial of service (DoS) is a very common attack. It may slow down or totally interrupt the service of a system.  Attacks Threatening Availability

slides.text: ﻿ SYMMETRIC CIPHER MODEL

﻿ SYMMETRIC CIPHER MODEL A symmetric encryption scheme has five ingredients :
Plaintext: the original intelligible message or data that is fed into the algorithm as input.
Encryption algorithm: The algorithm that performs various substitutions and transformations on the plaintext.
Secret key: an input to the encryption algorithm. The key is a value independent of the plaintext and of the algorithm. The algorithm will produce a different output depending on the specific key being used at the time. The exact substitutions and transformations performed by the algorithm depend on the key.
Ciphertext: This is the scrambled message produced as output. It depends on the plaintext and the secret key. For a given message, two different keys will produce two different ciphertexts. The ciphertext is an apparently random stream of data and, as it stands, is unintelligible.
Decryption algorithm: This is essentially the encryption algorithm run in reverse. It takes the ciphertext and the secret key and produces the original plaintext.
﻿ Why Symmetric?

﻿ SYMMETRIC CIPHER MODEL Dimensions of Cryptography
The type of operations used for transforming plaintext to cyphertext

﻿ SYMMETRIC CIPHER MODEL As cryptography is the science and art of creating secret codes, cryptanalysis is the science and art of breaking those codes. 
The users of an encryption algorithm can strive for an algorithm that meets one or both of the following criteria:
The cost of breaking the cipher exceeds the value of the encrypted information.
The time required to break the cipher exceeds the useful lifetime of the information.

﻿ SYMMETRIC CIPHER MODEL Kerckhoff’s Principle
One should always assume that the adversary knows the encryption/decryption algorithm. 
The resistance of the cipher to any attack must be based only on the secrecy of the key.

﻿ PLAYFAIR CIPHER Used by British Army in World war-I
The secret key is 5×5 matrix of 25 alphabets. (I & J) are considered the same. 
Different arrangements of letters can create many different secret keys. 
 Ref: Cryptography and Network Security by Behrouz Forouzan

rects.text: Cryptography and Network Security by Behrouz

slides.text:
﻿ RULES OF PLAYFAIR CIPHER Before Encryption:
If two letters in a pair are same, add a bogus letter (E.g.: ll,rr)
If number of characters in plaintext are odd, add one bogus character at the end
Encryption Rules:
If two letters in a pair are in the same row of secret key, the encrypted letter is the next letter to the right in the same row (with wrapping)
If two letters in a pair are in same column, the encrypted letter is the letter beneath it in the same column (with wrapping)
If the two letters in a pair are not in the same row or column, the encrypted letter is a letter that is in its own row but in the same column as the other letter
 Ref: Cryptography and Network Security by Behrouz Forouzan

﻿ VIGENERE CIPHER Designed by Blaise de Vigenere, a french mathematician
The key stream depends on the position of the character in the plaintext
Example: 
Encrypt the message “She is listening” using the 6-character keyword “PASCAL”.

﻿ VIGENERE CIPHER Solution: 
Find number of characters in the keyword. E.g. k=6
Break the plaintext in blocks of size ‘k’, identify values of each letter.
Prepare and repeat the keystream as required. 
                   For keyword, PASCAL, keystream is 15 00 18 02 00 11
Perform Encryption
